newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FOCUS - Portugal rejects IMF austerity plea.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Portugal rejects IMF austerity plea.

text.p: Portugal's government on Tuesday dismissed International Monetary Fund (IMF) suggestions that it must impose a wage freeze and public service layoffs to meet economic targets for joining a single European currency.

Antonio Pina Moura, secretary of state in the Prime Minister's office, said the Socialist government would cut its deficit to the three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) threshhold for economic and monetary union (EMU) without such draconian steps.
"We do not agree with the measures that the IMF suggests to guarantee budget targets," Pina Moura said in a radio interview.

The government believed it could award public servants with wage increases slightly above inflation without cutting jobs or raising taxes in 1997, and still meet the deficit criteria for EMU, he said.
He was commenting on a report in the Diario Economico newspaper about a confidential IMF study which said that Portugal could meet the deficit goal but only if it took tough action.
His comments were generally supported by independent analysts polled by Reuters who said the country should manage to achieve the necessary budget reductions without massive sacrifices.
The Fund recommended a freeze on public sector wages, a reduction in the number of public sector employees and cuts in current spending by ministries.
"Our projections indicate that the mere freezing in nominal terms...will not be enough," the Fund was quoted as saying.
Cutting the budget deficit to three percent of GDP in 1997 is one of the key entry criteria for the European Union's planned single currency.

Portugal's Socialist government, which is forecasting the deficit will fall to around four percent of GDP this year from some five percent in 1995, argues the EMU target can be achieved without huge sacrifices.

Diario Economico reported the IMF study, drawn up after a visit to Portugal in July, said the alternative to real cuts in spending was higher taxes, something the government has consistently rejected.
It recommended a rise in Value Added Tax (VAT) as the levels currently applied in Portugal were below European averages.
Analysts said that the strengthening of economic growth, improved tax collection and moderate 1997 public sector wage increases should make it possible to achieve this goal.

"If the economy grows at rates above 2.5 percent and if there is greater efficiency in the tax system and moderate public sector wage increases, it will be possible to meet the three percent budget deficit target next year," said Isabel Cabral, economist with Lisbon broker Fincor.
Jose Luiz Alzola, an analyst with Salomon Brothers in London, said he believed Portugal could hit the three percent target.
"It is possible," he said. "The government will have to make further adjustments to spending and taxation, but not much."
Most analysts said they believed that public sector layoffs and significant tax increases were unlikely.
Finance Minister Antonio Sousa Franco told parliament last week the government would not raise taxes in 1997 for the second straight year.
"It is a little hasty of the IMF to talk of layoffs in the public sector or tax rises," said Fincor's Cabral.
Analysts expect a further easing of key interest rates, which would reduce the burden of public sector debt service payments and boost prospects for meeting the deficit target.
